sentences: A young man in a broad black hat turns his body slightly and looks straight at us.
Under his upturned moustache, a faint smile plays on his lips.
His left hand rests on his hip, and a richly embroidered sleeve fills the lower part of the picture.
This portrait was painted in 1624 by the Dutch artist Frans Hals and is known as The Laughing Cavalier.
It is oil on canvas, 83 centimetres high and about 67 centimetres wide.
It hangs in the Wallace Collection in London, which calls it the most famous painting Hals ever made.
Hals was born around 1582 in Antwerp.
When he was a small child, his family moved north to Haarlem to escape the turmoil of war, and he worked there for the rest of his life.
He died in Haarlem in 1666.
Look at the top right corner.
A short Latin inscription says that he was 26 years old, in the year 1624.
But his name appears nowhere.
Scholars have suggested names, but no one knows for certain who he was.
The title has a story too.
Hals never gave the picture this name.
In a London exhibition catalogue of the 1870s it was simply called A Cavalier, and by around 1888 it had become The Laughing Cavalier.
Yet the man is not laughing.
His lips are closed in a smile, and we do not even know whether he was a soldier.
Now look at his face.
The upturned moustache makes the smile look wider than it really is.
His eyes look straight ahead, so wherever you stand, they seem to follow you.
Look closely at the embroidery on his sleeve.
You can find bees, arrows, flaming horns of plenty, lovers' knots and tongues of fire.
In his time, these were signs of the pleasures and pains of love.
The costume itself follows the latest French fashion, which only the Dutch elite could afford.
Step closer, and the fine lace and embroidery break up into long, quick brushstrokes.
The black clothes are not one flat black either.
Vincent van Gogh, full of admiration, said that Hals must have had twenty-seven different blacks.
In 1865, at an auction in Paris, the 4th Marquess of Hertford bought the painting after a bidding battle with Baron James de Rothschild.
His collection was later given to the British nation and became the Wallace Collection.
Step back and take in the whole portrait.
His name and his work are lost, but the confident look of a young man of 26 has lasted four hundred years.
Today, try giving the face in the mirror a small, knowing smile.
